passage: The results came out during a wedding, of all places, in a hot, noisy hall full of relatives. Mohit got 71 percent. His cousin got 94. Before Mohit could even eat, Bade Papa announced, "Our Mohit will never be like his cousin," and a few uncles nodded. It wasn't the first time. Mohit had heard it since he was eight, and lately he had started saying it first: "I'm the average one." He slipped out to the parking area. His mother, Sudha, found him there, her sari pinned up, holding two plates. "Seventy-one, without tuition, and with your leg in plaster for a month," she said. "I watched how hard you worked. That's who you are." Mohit stared at the plate. Then, slowly, he took it.

qa.q: What percentage did Mohit get?
qa.a: 71 percent.

qa.q: Why had Mohit started calling himself "the average one"?
qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and discouraged after hearing since he was eight that he would never be like his cousin, until the repeated verdict became how he saw himself.

qa.q: What did Sudha choose to point out in the parking area, and why might it help?
qa.a: She named his real effort, no tuition and a leg in plaster, and said that is who he is, giving him a different, hopeful story about himself. 🤍

qa.q: How might the relatives' words feel to Mohit's cousin?
qa.a: The cousin is being used as a measuring stick, which might bring pride but also pressure, and could make it awkward to be close to Mohit.

grounding: A teenager who keeps hearing he will never be like his cousin has started to believe it, while his mother's steady belief in his effort offers another view.

passage: In the Pune flat, the cousin's photo with the district chess trophy stood on Dadi's shelf. "Dhruv, you'll never be like Neel," Dadi said most Sundays, not unkindly, as if reading out the weather. Dhruv had stopped playing chess at thirteen. At sixteen, when a teacher suggested the school team, he said, "Not my thing. Neel's the smart one." That evening his father, Manoj, set up the old board on the dining table. "One game. I'm rusty." Dhruv won in twenty moves. Manoj didn't mention Neel. He only said, "You saw that knight fork three moves ahead. That's practice, not magic. You could do more of that if you wanted." Dhruv put the pieces back slowly, looking at the knight.

qa.q: Where did Manoj set up the old chess board?
qa.a: On the dining table.

qa.q: What does Dhruv saying "Neel's the smart one" suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: After years of hearing he'd never be like Neel, he has come to see himself as the less smart one and turns down chances before trying.

qa.q: What choice did Manoj make that could lift Dhruv?
qa.a: Instead of comparing, he played a game, praised one specific move and said it came from practice, showing steady belief that Dhruv could grow.

qa.q: Why might Dadi say it "as if reading out the weather"?
qa.a: To Dadi it may feel like a harmless remark rather than a verdict; she may not realise how much the repeated words have shaped what Dhruv thinks he can do.

grounding: A teenager who keeps hearing he will never match his cousin gives up chess, while his father's quiet belief in practice offers a way back.

"Sunaina, Papa's home! Show him the science marks."
"Why? He'll just say Ritika got more."
Vikas put down his bag. "Who said I'd say that?"
"Everyone. Chachi, Mummy, you. 'Sunaina, you'll never be like Ritika.'"
"I said that?"
"At Diwali. And the summer before."
Vikas sat on the arm of the sofa. "What did you get?"
"Sixty-two. I'm the not-Ritika one. It's fine."
"It's not fine if you believe it." He paused. "I shouldn't have said it. I'm sorry."
Sunaina shrugged, but she looked up.
"Ritika works hard. So can you. Want to go through the paper tonight? I'm not great at science, but I'm good at sitting beside you."
"Okay. Only if you don't compare."
"Deal. No Ritika at this table."

qa.q: What did Sunaina score in science?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: Why does Sunaina call herself "the not-Ritika one"?
qa.a: She has heard "you'll never be like Ritika" so often, even from Papa, that she has taken it on as who she is. Her shrug and "It's fine" hide how hurt she feels.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation?
qa.a: Papa admitted he had said it, apologised and offered to sit with her over the paper with no comparing, replacing the verdict with belief in her effort.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling when he asks "I said that?"
qa.a: He seems shocked and a bit ashamed that a passing comment at Diwali stuck with her so deeply, which pushes him to apologise.

grounding: A teenage girl who keeps hearing she will never be like her cousin has adopted it as her identity, until her father apologises and offers steady belief.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: For years, at every family wedding, I was the other niece, and it came with the same line. 'Rehana, you'll never be like Zainab.' Zainab, my cousin, topped her school and read English novels at eight. The aunties said it with a smile, as if it were a small joke. By fourteen I'd started saying it before they did: 'I'm not the studious one.' It was easier. I stopped trying in Urdu essays and told myself I was just 'not that type'. My Ammi never said the line. Instead, every night after dinner, she sat with me at the kitchen table while I wrote one paragraph. Just one. She'd read it and say, 'Better than yesterday.' She never compared. Last month my essay was read aloud in class. Walking home, I realised I hadn't thought about Zainab all day. I'm still not Zainab. I'm starting to think I don't have to be.

qa.q: What did Rehana's Ammi do every night after dinner?
qa.a: She sat with Rehana at the kitchen table while Rehana wrote one paragraph, and said, 'Better than yesterday.'

qa.q: Why did Rehana start saying 'I'm not the studious one' herself?
qa.a: After hearing the line for years, it felt easier to say it first than to be hurt by it, so she slowly took it on as who she was.

qa.q: What did Ammi do differently from the aunties, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ammi never compared and focused on small daily effort, which showed Rehana she could improve and quietly lifted her.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Rehana if they heard her essay read aloud?
qa.a: They might be surprised, since their joke had fixed her as the less studious cousin without noticing her effort.

grounding: A teenage girl who kept hearing she'd never be like her cousin took it on as identity, until her mother's steady belief in effort quietly lifted her.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Ayesha, Class 10, Thursday:
Keerthana came in after missing two basketball practices. She said, 'What's the point? At home everyone says I'll never be like Divya.' Divya is her cousin, captain of the district team. Keerthana said her grandmother tells her this most Sundays, kindly, as a fact. She now calls herself 'the lazy one' and laughed when she said it, but did not look up. When I asked who else at home talks about basketball, she said her father drives her to every practice and always asks, 'What did you learn today?' She said, 'He doesn't care if I'm Divya. He just wants to know what I learned.' She smiled for the first time then. Next step: I've invited her father for a short meeting to talk about how to keep that steady focus on effort going.

qa.q: Who is Divya?
qa.a: Divya is Keerthana's cousin, captain of the district team.

qa.q: What does Keerthana laughing but not looking up suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests the label 'the lazy one' hurts her, even while she tries to make it sound like a joke.

qa.q: What is the counsellor's next step, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: The counsellor invited her father for a meeting, to strengthen his steady focus on effort, which already makes Keerthana smile.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's father see her, compared with her grandmother?
qa.a: Her father sees Keerthana as someone learning and growing at practice, while her grandmother measures her against Divya.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenage girl absorbing a family verdict that she'll never match her cousin, and her father's steady interest in effort quietly lifting her.
